content: Quaternium-15 is a chemical preservative commonly used in a wide range of cosmetic and industrial products. It functions as a formaldehyde-releasing agent, which helps prevent microbial growth and extends the shelf life of these products. This compound is present in various items, including mascara, eyeliner, moisturizers, lotions, shampoos, conditioners, nail polishes, personal lubricants, soaps, body washes, baby lotions or shampoos, facial cleansers, tanning oils, self-tanning creams, sunscreens, powders, shaving products, ointments, personal wipes or cleansers, as well as industrial products like wipes, paper, inks, paints, polishes, waxes, and lubricants. Quaternium-15 has the potential to cause contact dermatitis, which is an inflammatory skin reaction resulting from an allergic response. This reaction is more likely to occur in individuals with sensitive skin, infants, or when the compound comes into contact with particularly sensitive areas of the body, such as the genital region. The chemical structure of quaternium-15 is represented by the formula C9H16Cl2N4. It is also marketed under various alternative names, including Dowicil 75, Dowicil 100, Dowco 184, Dowicide Q, 1-(3-Chloroallyl)-3,5,7-triaza-1-azoniaadamantane chloride, N-(3-chloroallyl) hexaminium chloride, hexamethylenetetramine chloroallyl chloride, 3,5,7-Triaza-1-azoniaadamantane, and 1-(3-chloroallyl)-chloride. Other preservatives that release formaldehyde and share similar properties with quaternium-15 include imidazolidinyl urea (commonly sold as Germall®), diazolidinyl urea (Germall II®), DMDM hydantoin (Glydant®), bromonitropropane diol (Bronopol™), tris(hydroxymethyl) nitromethane (Tris Nitro®), and sodium hydroxymethylglycinate. Quaternium-15 is recognized as an allergen and is known to cause contact dermatitis in individuals who are sensitive to it. Many people who are allergic to quaternium-15 also exhibit allergic reactions to formaldehyde, as the two are closely related. The presence of an allergy to quaternium-15 can be confirmed through a diagnostic patch test, which involves applying the substance to the skin and monitoring for a reaction.
